title: Operations Foundations
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Operations management is the design and control of the processes that transform inputs into goods and services. The transformation model: Inputs (materials, labor, capital) → Process → Outputs, with feedback loops. Four operational objectives, often in tension: cost, quality, speed, flexibility. Little's Law is fundamental: Inventory = Throughput × Flow Time — reduce flow time or inventory and the relationship holds. A process is only as fast as its bottleneck; improving anything but the bottleneck adds no throughput.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A coffee shop serves 30 customers/hour, and on average 5 customers are in the system. Little's Law gives flow time = 5/30 hour = 10 minutes per customer. To cut wait time, you either speed throughput or reduce the number in the system — the math tells you which lever to pull.

PRACTICE: 1) Map a process you know as Inputs → Process → Outputs. 2) Identify its bottleneck. 3) Apply Little's Law to estimate flow time from throughput and inventory.

title: Process Design & Analysis
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Process types on a spectrum: job shop (high variety, low volume) → batch → assembly line → continuous flow (low variety, high volume). Cycle time is the time between outputs; takt time is the pace of customer demand (available time / demand). Match cycle time to takt time — faster wastes capacity, slower fails demand. Capacity = 1/cycle time of the bottleneck. Process mapping and value stream mapping expose waste. Utilization above ~85% causes queue times to explode nonlinearly (queuing theory).

WORKED EXAMPLE: Demand is 480 units/day over an 8-hour shift → takt time = 480 min / 480 units = 1 minute/unit. If any workstation takes longer than 60 seconds, it's the bottleneck and demand won't be met. Balancing every station to ≤60 seconds is the design goal.

PRACTICE: 1) Calculate takt time for a given demand and shift. 2) Identify which station is the bottleneck. 3) Explain why running at 95% utilization increases wait times.

title: Lean & Waste Elimination
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Lean, from the Toyota Production System, targets the 8 wastes (DOWNTIME): Defects, Overproduction, Waiting, Non-utilized talent, Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Extra-processing. Just-In-Time (JIT) produces only what's needed, when needed, pulled by demand (kanban) rather than pushed by forecast. Kaizen is continuous incremental improvement by the people doing the work. 5S (Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain) creates a disciplined workplace. Jidoka: stop the line when a defect appears so it's fixed at the source, not passed downstream.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A factory overproduces to 'stay efficient,' building inventory that hides quality problems and ties up cash. Switching to pull-based JIT reveals defects immediately (no buffer to hide them) and frees working capital — overproduction was the root waste feeding all the others.

PRACTICE: 1) Identify examples of 3 of the 8 wastes in a process. 2) Design a simple kanban pull signal. 3) Apply 5S to a workspace.

title: Quality Management
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Quality is conformance to requirements and fitness for use. Statistical Process Control (SPC) uses control charts to distinguish common-cause variation (inherent, leave it alone) from special-cause variation (fix it) — reacting to common-cause noise makes things worse (tampering). Six Sigma targets 3.4 defects per million (DMAIC: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control). Cost of quality: prevention and appraisal costs are cheap; failure costs (internal and external) are expensive — invest upstream. The Pareto principle: ~80% of defects come from ~20% of causes.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A manager adjusts a machine every time a measurement drifts slightly, believing they're improving quality. SPC reveals the drift is common-cause noise — their 'corrections' actually increase variation. Doing nothing (leaving common-cause alone) produces better quality than constant tampering.

PRACTICE: 1) Distinguish common vs special cause in a data pattern. 2) Build a Pareto chart of defect causes. 3) Explain why prevention beats inspection economically.

title: Supply Chain & Inventory
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The supply chain spans suppliers → manufacturing → distribution → customer. The bullwhip effect: small demand changes amplify upstream, causing wild swings — reduced by sharing real demand data. Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) balances ordering cost against holding cost: EOQ = √(2DS/H). Safety stock buffers demand variability; reorder point = (demand × lead time) + safety stock. Inventory turns = COGS / average inventory — higher is more efficient but risks stockouts. ABC analysis focuses control on the vital few high-value items.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A retailer sees demand vary by ±5%, but orders to its supplier swing ±40% because each tier adds buffer and reacts to the tier below. Sharing point-of-sale data up the chain collapses the bullwhip — the amplification was an information problem, not a demand problem.

PRACTICE: 1) Calculate EOQ from demand, order cost, and holding cost. 2) Determine a reorder point with safety stock. 3) Explain how data sharing reduces the bullwhip effect.

title: Capacity, Scheduling & Constraints
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: The Theory of Constraints (Goldratt): every system has one binding constraint; throughput is governed by it. Five focusing steps: Identify the constraint, Exploit it (maximize its use), Subordinate everything else to it, Elevate it (add capacity), then Repeat. Never optimize a non-constraint — it just builds inventory. Capacity strategies: lead (build ahead of demand), lag (follow demand), match. Scheduling rules trade off objectives: shortest-processing-time minimizes average wait; earliest-due-date minimizes lateness.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A plant buys a faster machine for a non-bottleneck station, expecting more output. Throughput doesn't change — the bottleneck elsewhere still caps everything, and now inventory piles up before it. The Theory of Constraints predicts exactly this: improving a non-constraint is worse than useless.

PRACTICE: 1) Apply the five focusing steps to a constrained process. 2) Choose a capacity strategy (lead/lag/match) for a scenario. 3) Explain why local efficiency can hurt global throughput.

title: Grandmaster — Operations Strategy
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: Operations strategy aligns the operating system with competitive priorities — you cannot be best at cost, quality, speed, and flexibility simultaneously; you make deliberate trade-offs (Skinner's focused factory). The sand cone model argues quality must come first, then dependability, then speed, then cost — built cumulatively, not traded. Order qualifiers (table stakes to compete) vs order winners (why customers choose you). Global operations balance efficiency (centralize) against responsiveness (localize). Digital operations (IoT, predictive maintenance, digital twins) shift from reactive to predictive.

WORKED EXAMPLE: A company tries to match a low-cost rival on price while also matching a premium rival on customization. It ends up mediocre at both — 'stuck in the middle' operationally. Choosing one competitive priority and designing the whole operation around it beats trying to win on every dimension.

PRACTICE: 1) Identify a company's order winners vs qualifiers. 2) Choose a single operational priority and design around it. 3) Assess an efficiency-vs-responsiveness trade-off.

title: King Level — Operational Excellence & Transformation
content:
KEY CONCEPTS: At the highest level, operations becomes a source of durable competitive advantage that rivals cannot easily copy — because it's embedded in thousands of interlocking decisions and culture, not a single feature. Operational excellence: reliability so complete it becomes a brand promise (think of operations-led companies whose delivery IS their moat). Continuous improvement as culture, not program — everyone improves their work daily. Resilience engineering: designing for disruption (redundancy, flexibility, rapid recovery) as climate and geopolitics raise volatility. The King-level truth: strategy sets direction, but operations determines whether you can actually deliver it — most strategies die in execution.

WORKED EXAMPLE: Two retailers have identical strategies. One wins for a decade because its operations — inventory accuracy, replenishment speed, cost per shipment — are 20% better across ten thousand small processes. No single advantage is copyable; the cumulative operational system is the moat. Excellence compounds.

PRACTICE: 1) Identify an operations-led company and its operational moat. 2) Design a continuous-improvement culture mechanism. 3) Build a resilience plan for one critical supply disruption.
